study.title: Predicting acupuncture efficacy for neck pain based on functional connectivity features: a machine learning study
study.study_design: Prospective cohort study with machine learning prediction model and longitudinal fMRI analysis; clinical data and functional magnetic resonance imaging scans collected pre- and post-treatment
study.population: Patients with neck pain recruited from the campus of Shanxi University of Chinese Medicine and the Shanxi Provincial Hospital of Acupuncture between March 2023 and May 2024
study.inclusion_criteria: 1) primarily complained of NP with a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain severity score of more than 3 points (out of a possible 10), 2) had experienced symptoms for no more than 3 months, 3) were between 18 and 60 years old and right-handed, and 4) were willing to provide informed consent
study.exclusion_criteria: 1) pregnant or breastfeeding women, 2) individuals with serious primary health conditions or psychiatric/neurological disorders, 3) those who had MRI contraindications, and 4) participants enrolled in other clinical trials

extraction_notes.note: Expectancy, credibility, and blinding success were not assessed or reported in this study. There is no sham control group, so blinding/credibility measures are not applicable, but expectancy was also not measured.
Adverse events were not reported in the paper. No statement about safety outcomes was found.

The study does not include a sham acupuncture or placebo control group. All 80 patients received real acupuncture; responders and non-responders were classified post-hoc based on VAS improvement ≥21%. This limits causal inference about acupuncture-specific effects versus non-specific effects.

Deqi was intended ('with the aim of achieving the Deqi sensation') but no formal deqi assessment instrument (e.g., MASS, Southampton Needle Sensation Questionnaire) was reported. No quantitative deqi data are available for extraction.

Supplementary Material 1 referenced in text: 'A comprehensive breakdown of these predictive features and their respective weights can be found in Supplementary Material 1.' Only the top 5 features are reported in the main text; the full list of 117 predictive features and weights is in a supplement not provided in this PDF.

The direction of within-group changes in Table 2 (responders) and Table 3 (non-responders) requires interpretation. The paper states non-responders showed 'significant decreases after treatment' (Table 3 text), yet all statistic values are positive. For responders (Table 2), text states 'marked reduction' for row 1 (positive statistic = 2.206) and 'notable increases' for rows 2-6 (negative statistics). The sign of the statistic may reflect the direction of the test coding (post minus pre), not the standard t-statistic sign. These directions have been preserved as described in the text.

Statistical test type for longitudinal pre-post comparisons within groups is not explicitly specified in Methods or Tables 2-3. The paper states 'intragroup comparisons before and after treatment were performed using paired samples t-tests or the Wilcoxon signed-rank test' — it is unclear which was used for each specific functional connectivity edge comparison.

For clinical outcomes in Table 1, only between-group post-treatment comparisons are shown (statistics and p-values). Within-group pre-post statistics are described narratively ('significant changes') but specific within-group test statistics and p-values are not tabulated. Only between-group statistics at post-treatment are extractable from Table 1.

The 117 predictive consistency features are referenced as the feature set used in the SVM model but only 5 top-weighted features are reported in the main text. The full list is in Supplementary Material 1 not provided. Therefore, only 5 feature weights were extractable.

The paper does not explicitly state the exact number of features selected for longitudinal and correlation analyses. The text implies all 117 predictive consistency features were examined for longitudinal changes, but the optimal model used 217 features. The 117 'consistent' features are a subset identified across LOOCV iterations.

No MNI coordinates are reported for any neuroimaging results. All results are reported as functional connectivity edges (pairs of AAL116 regions), not as peak/cluster coordinates. No coordinate-level extraction is possible.
The filtering parameters (bandpass filtering frequency range) for the resting-state fMRI preprocessing are not reported.
Global signal regression status is not reported.
Fisher Z transformation was not applied to functional connectivity data. The paper acknowledges this as a deviation from conventional preprocessing in the Limitations section.

The within-group test statistics for VAS, SAS, SDS intragroup comparisons (paired t-test or Wilcoxon) are not provided in Table 1. Only the between-group comparison statistics at post-treatment are extractable.

The study design classifies responders vs non-responders within a single acupuncture treatment cohort (not randomized). The SVM model is trained on pre-treatment FC to predict this post-hoc classification. The two 'arms' reflect a data-driven stratification, not a randomized allocation.

The study mentions 90 enrolled, 83 completing the two-week program and post-treatment fMRI scan, 3 removed for excessive head motion, yielding 80 analyzed. However, dropout details (reasons for 7 withdrawals between enrollment and completion) are not reported.
